thread.title: Stressed-out stock traders face Friday hurdles posed by jobs report, Fed’s Powell - MarketWatch

author: Sunny Oh
title: Stressed-out stock traders face Friday hurdles posed by jobs report, Fed’s Powell - MarketWatch
text:
With stocks already off to a rough start in 2019, shellshocked investors face a pair of potentially make-or-break events on Friday: the all-important December jobs report and a public appearance by Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell.
Both come as attention is focused on the Fed amid growing doubts over its ability to stick to its forecast of two rate increases next year without further stoking concerns over a potential recession.
“We look for Powell to soften his tone and indicate…that the Fed will be flexible in adjusting their economic and rate outlook in the face of changing economic and financial conditions without pledging to pause for a defined period of time,” said Kathy Bostjancic, head of U.S. financial market economics at Oxford Economics, in a Thursday note.
The December jobs report is set for release at 8:30 a.m. Eastern, while Powell is set to take part in a panel discussion at 10:15 a.m. Eastern alongside his predecessors Janet Yellen and Ben Bernanke at the annual meeting of the American Economic Association in Atlanta.
Market participants are in need of reassurance, after the Dow DJIA, -2.83% and the S&P 500 SPX, -2.48% got off to their worst beginning to a new year since 2000 .
But economists said the Fed and the jobs report could end up working against each other as senior Fed officials try to communicate a slower pace of hikes this year even as the solid labor market puts pressure on the central bank to stay the course.
Trading on Friday could get volatile as investors watch how Powell acknowledges the rising risks to the U.S. economy, said Charlie Ripley, a money manager at Allianz Investment Management.
See : U.S. may find ray of light in December jobs report amid gathering economic clouds
To be sure, stronger-than-expected job gains would help stave off fears of a recession and demonstrate the U.S.’s resilience to global growth headwinds amid a torrent of lackluster data around the world. This week, investors dealt with survey data pointing to manufacturing slowdowns in the eurozone and China. U.S. stocks ended sharply lower Thursday after Apple AAPL, -9.96% announced that it would cut its revenue guidance because of weakness in China and the Institute for Supply Management’s manufacturing index pointed to a sharper-than-expected slowdown in domestic activity.
“The December employment report should provide significant reassurance that the economy is holding up far better than market participants currently perceive,” wrote Stephen Stanley, chief economist at Amherst Pierpont Securities.
Analysts polled by MarketWatch expect the report to show the U.S. economy added 182,000 jobs in December, a jump from the 155,00 created the previous month.
But with investors still wary of the prospect of an obstinate Fed, a solid employment report could contribute to the perception that the central bank will keep raising rates at the steady pace seen throughout 2018, renewing the same fears that had pushed stocks off their all-time highs in October.
Still, a robust labor market haven’t stopped investors from betting against the Fed’s hikes due to the sharp tightening of financial conditions after risk assets began selling off at the end of the year.
The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average are down nearly 17% and 16%, respectively, from their all-time highs, while yields for investment-grade corporate debt has risen to their highest levels in several years.
“The risks are skewed to a longer pause in the first half of the year than we thought just a month ago due to the recent tightening in financial conditions,” wrote economists at Wells Fargo.
Some traders have ramped up bets on the central bank to cut interest rates in the middle of this year, a far cry from when they had priced in two rate increases in 2019.
Bostjancic highlighted that the 2-year Treasury yield TMUBMUSD02Y, +1.17% has now fallen below the 12-month Treasury bill TMUBMUSD01Y, +0.72% suggesting investors are pricing in monetary easing in 2020.
